Family Health

Vaginal and vulvar cancer: diagnosis and specialist care

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Vaginal cancer and vulvar cancer affect different parts of the body. A suspicious change needs a diagnosis before anyone can choose treatment: where did it begin, what cells are involved, and has it spread? Many genital symptoms have noncancerous causes, but persistent changes deserve examination even after a normal cervical screening result.

Two nearby sites, with different cancer pathways

The vagina is the internal passage connecting the cervix to the outside of the body. The vulva is external: it includes the labia, clitoris and the area around the vaginal opening. The cervix is a separate structure at the lower end of the uterus. A cancer beside the opening is not automatically vaginal cancer; its precise starting point matters.

Primary vaginal cancer starts in the vaginal tissue and is rare. Cancer found there more often represents spread from another site, such as the cervix or uterine lining. That distinction changes the diagnosis and treatment plan. A previous cancer, hysterectomy or radiotherapy history should therefore be part of the specialist assessment, rather than assuming that any new vaginal tumour is a new primary cancer.

Risk factors do not predict an individual diagnosis

Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, or HPV, contributes to many squamous cancers of the vagina and vulva. Vulvar cancer can also develop through an HPV-independent pathway, sometimes alongside lichen sclerosus and particular precancerous skin changes. Older age, smoking, weakened immunity and a history of genital precancer or cancer may affect risk, but younger people can also be affected.

Changes in the genes of tumour cells do not, by themselves, mean that a cancer was inherited from a parent. An HPV-related diagnosis is not a reason for blame. HPV vaccination can reduce HPV-related risk, and stopping smoking is helpful, but neither replaces assessment of a new lesion. People with diagnosed vulvar skin disease still need their own treatment and review plan.

Prenatal DES exposure and uncommon cell types

Exposure before birth to diethylstilbestrol, or DES, is associated with a rare clear-cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina or cervix. This refers to a medicine taken by a person’s mother during pregnancy. The increased risk does not mean that every exposed person will develop cancer; the absolute risk remains low.

Tell your clinician about known prenatal DES exposure so surveillance can be individualized. Age, previous surgery and earlier findings affect the plan. Clear-cell cancer is different from the more common squamous cancer, and rare tumours such as melanoma or sarcoma need their own specialist approach. A colour change alone cannot establish which type of lesion is present.

Symptoms need examination, not just a screening test

Arrange an assessment for bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause, unusual persistent discharge, a vaginal lump or persistent pelvic pain. On the vulva, a continuing itch, new lump, ulcer, bleeding area or changing patch of skin also deserves examination. These signs have many possible explanations. Do not wait for a sore to remain for a full month before asking for help, or keep treating a changing lesion as thrush without review.

A normal Pap or HPV screening result does not rule out vaginal or vulvar cancer. There is no routine screening test for these cancers in people without symptoms; selected surveillance after precancer, cancer or prenatal DES exposure is a different situation. Very heavy bleeding, or feeling faint or likely to pass out with bleeding, needs emergency help. Do not wait for a cancer-clinic appointment in that situation.

What examination and biopsy can establish

A clinician will ask about the change, examine the relevant area and explain any internal examination. Magnification may help identify where to take a sample: examination of vulvar skin is often called vulvoscopy, while colposcopy can examine the cervix and vagina. Ask about a chaperone, support person and ways to reduce discomfort. An examination can be paused or stopped; it should not be promised to be painless.

A biopsy removes a small tissue sample for a pathologist to examine. Local anaesthetic is commonly used for a vulvar sample. When vulvar cancer is suspected, a planned punch or incisional biopsy often preserves options for later treatment better than simply removing the entire lesion first. Separate suspicious areas may need separate samples. The specialist should explain how and when results will be communicated.

Understanding the pathology result

The report should clarify whether the sample shows a benign condition, a precancerous change or invasive cancer. Invasion means abnormal cells have grown beyond the surface layer into deeper tissue. The cell type and, where relevant, HPV-associated features help the team classify the disease. A laboratory result must be interpreted alongside the examination and the exact site sampled.

Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, or VIN, and vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, or VaIN, describe precancerous changes in different locations. They are not interchangeable names for invasive cancer. If the sample does not explain a concerning lesion, further assessment or another biopsy may be needed. Ask for the actual diagnosis in writing rather than relying on the general phrase “abnormal cells”.

Staging tests are selected for the finding

After cancer is confirmed, staging assesses its extent. The questions include how far it has grown locally, whether nearby organs are involved, and whether lymph nodes or more distant areas are affected. Vaginal and vulvar cancers have their own staging systems. The stage is different from the cell type or grade described by the pathologist.

A pelvic MRI may help map local vaginal disease; CT, PET-CT or groin ultrasound may answer other specific questions. An examination under anaesthesia or a look inside the bladder or rectum is sometimes useful when involvement is suspected. These are not a compulsory checklist for every person. Ask what each proposed test could change about the treatment decision.

Treatment when cancer begins in the vagina

Care should be planned by a team experienced in gynaecological cancers. The site, size, extent and cell type matter, along with previous treatment, health and personal priorities. Selected small, early tumours may be treated surgically. Radiotherapy is an important option and can combine treatment from outside the body with brachytherapy, which places a radiation source close to the tumour.

Chemotherapy may be given with radiotherapy in some situations. More advanced or recurrent disease may need a different combination or a clinical-trial discussion. There is no universal sequence of surgery followed by chemotherapy and radiation for everyone. If the vaginal lesion is spread from another cancer, the plan must address that original cancer and its prior treatment.

Treatment when cancer begins in the vulva

Many early vulvar cancers are treated by removing the tumour with an appropriate margin of surrounding tissue. This does not automatically mean removal of the whole vulva. The operation is planned around cancer control and preservation of function, with reconstruction when needed. Larger or more extensive disease may require radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surgery or a combination.

Groin lymph-node assessment is a separate decision. Sentinel-node biopsy can be suitable for selected early cancers; others need a different nodal approach. A scan alone cannot always exclude microscopic involvement. Ask why the proposed procedure is suitable, whether one or both groins are involved, and what it means for wound recovery and the risk of lasting leg or genital swelling.

Why treatment for precancer is different

A prescription cream is not a substitute for diagnosing a suspicious lesion. Some HPV-associated high-grade VIN can be treated with specialist-supervised imiquimod, laser treatment or surgery after invasive cancer has been excluded. The choice depends on the type, extent and location, as well as the person’s preferences and ability to attend follow-up. Treatment can irritate the skin and needs review.

Differentiated VIN, often associated with an HPV-independent pathway, generally calls for surgical excision rather than assuming the same cream options apply. VaIN has its own grade- and site-specific management. Neither a treatment response nor a previous precancer diagnosis means a new lesion can be ignored. These local treatments should not be described as cures for invasive vaginal or vulvar cancer.

Function, fertility and follow-up belong in the plan

Before treatment, discuss possible effects on fertility, ovarian function, urination, bowel function and sexual comfort. If future pregnancy matters to you, request fertility advice before treatment begins; preservation options depend on the cancer and treatment and may not be feasible. Reconstructive care, specialist nursing and psychological support can also be part of cancer care, rather than something to seek only after problems develop.

Follow-up is individualized. It may include symptom review and examination, with scans when indicated, as well as care for vulvar skin disease, scarring, vaginal narrowing or lymphoedema. After pelvic radiotherapy, the team may discuss lubricants, vaginal rehabilitation or other symptom treatment suited to you. Report new symptoms between appointments instead of waiting for the next routine visit.

Outlook and questions for the specialist

These cancers can be life-threatening, but a diagnosis does not mean death is inevitable. Earlier, localized disease can often be treated successfully. Outlook depends on the original site, stage, cell type, lymph-node involvement, response to treatment and general health. Population survival figures cannot tell one person exactly what will happen. When cure is not possible, treatment and supportive care can still help control symptoms and meet personal goals.

Useful questions include: Is this a primary cancer or spread from elsewhere? Is it precancer or invasive disease? Which findings determine my stage? What is the aim of each treatment, and what alternatives are reasonable? Who will explain results and help with side effects? Leave with a contact plan for urgent problems, and ask for clarification or a second opinion if the diagnosis or proposed treatment remains unclear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The original site, tissue diagnosis and extent of disease guide specialist treatment; vaginal and vulvar cancers should not be treated as one condition.

Cervical screening and diagnostic investigation answer different questions. Persistent symptoms need assessment even when screening is up to date.

Precancer treatments and follow-up depend on the subtype; invasive cancer needs a specialist oncology plan.

How BeMama can help

Bring your previous pathology and cancer-treatment records if available. Ask the team to explain the exact site and tissue diagnosis, which tests will change care, and how treatment could affect daily life and future pregnancy.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment of persistent genital bleeding, a new or changing lesion, an ulcer or ongoing unexplained symptoms. Seek emergency help for very heavy bleeding or feeling faint or likely to pass out with bleeding. Do not wait for routine screening or a cancer-clinic appointment in an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The vagina, cervix and vulva are different sites; identifying where a cancer began is essential to planning care.
  • Persistent symptoms need examination even after normal cervical screening. Biopsy establishes the tissue diagnosis.
  • Precancer, invasive cancer and spread from another cancer require different decisions; no scan or treatment list fits everyone.
  • Discuss function, fertility, recovery and follow-up with a specialist team before treatment starts.
  • Very heavy bleeding or feeling faint with bleeding needs emergency help, rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Frequently asked questions

What causes vaginal cancer?

Many squamous vaginal cancers are linked to persistent high-risk HPV. Prenatal DES exposure is associated with the much rarer clear-cell type. Risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis, and a cancer found in the vagina may have spread from another organ rather than started there.

What symptoms can vaginal cancer cause?

Possible symptoms include bleeding after sex or menopause, unusual discharge, a lump and persistent pelvic pain; sometimes there are no early symptoms. These changes often have another cause, but need assessment. Very heavy bleeding or feeling faint with bleeding requires emergency help.

Is cancer at the vaginal opening the same as vaginal cancer?

Not necessarily. The surrounding external tissues belong to the vulva, while the vagina is the internal passage. Examination and the biopsy location help establish the starting site. The name matters because staging and treatment differ.

How is vulvar cancer diagnosed?

A clinician examines the area and takes a tissue biopsy from a suspicious lesion, sometimes using magnification to guide the assessment. A pathologist identifies the tissue changes. Scans or further examinations are selected when needed; they do not replace the biopsy diagnosis.

Can a normal smear test rule these cancers out?

No. Cervical screening does not provide a general test for vaginal or vulvar cancer. Symptoms still need diagnostic assessment. People with previous precancer, cancer or prenatal DES exposure may have an individualized surveillance plan.

Can a cream treat vulvar cancer?

A specialist may use imiquimod for selected HPV-associated high-grade vulvar precancer after excluding invasion. That is different from treating invasive cancer, and it is not the usual approach for differentiated VIN. Do not try a cream on a suspicious lesion instead of obtaining a diagnosis.

Will treatment remove the whole vulva or prevent pregnancy?

Neither outcome is automatic. Surgery can sometimes be localized, while other cancers require more extensive treatment. Effects on pregnancy depend on the organs involved and the treatments used. Discuss fertility and preservation possibilities before treatment, without assuming they will be possible for every cancer.

Are vaginal and vulvar cancers always fatal?

No. Some can be cured, especially when localized, while others need treatment aimed at controlling disease and symptoms. Your specialist can discuss prognosis using the confirmed site, stage, cell type and health information; a general survival statistic is not an individual prediction.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
